prompt: In a BPMN diagram, what does an event drawn with a thick border mean?
hint: The border says when in the process the event happens.

choices.text: It interrupts the activity it is attached to
choices.why: That is a boundary event with a solid double border; a thick single border is something else.

choices.text: Something happens partway through and the token waits there
choices.why: That is an intermediate event, and it has a double border.

choices.text: The path ends there
choices.why: Right: a thick border is an end event, and a process may have several, one per outcome.

choices.text: A message arriving starts a new instance
choices.why: That is a start event with a message marker, drawn with a thin border.

prompt: Match each shape to what it means in BPMN 2.0.
hint: Border, marker, then line style.

pairs.left: a circle with a double border
pairs.right: something happens partway through the process

pairs.left: a rounded rectangle with a small plus sign at the bottom
a diamond with a plus sign
pairs.right: a token leaves on every outgoing path

pairs.left: a dashed line leaving a small hollow circle
pairs.right: a message passing between two participants

right_distractors: the order of the steps inside one pool

prompt: Joana's first sketch had a diamond labelled "Check quality" with two arrows leaving it. What is wrong with it?
hint: Ask who does the checking.

choices.text: It should be an inclusive gateway, because a quality check can fail in several ways at once
choices.why: The kind of gateway is not the problem; whatever its marker, a gateway cannot do the checking.

choices.text: Checking is work, so it is a task; the diamond after it asks a question the task answered
choices.why: Right: a gateway does no work and only routes on what the work before it produced, so "approved?" follows a task.

choices.text: A gateway is labelled with the role that decides, here the quality team
choices.why: Roles belong to lanes; a gateway is labelled with a question.

choices.text: Two arrows are too few for a gateway
choices.why: A split with two outgoing flows is the ordinary case.

prompt: Halfway through onboarding, the process waits for the signed contract to come back from the farm. How is that point drawn?
hint: Where in the process, and does it catch or throw?

choices.text: An intermediate event with a hollow envelope
choices.why: Right: a double border for partway through, and a hollow marker because it catches.

choices.text: An intermediate event with a filled envelope
choices.why: A filled marker throws: that would send a message, not wait for one.

choices.text: A start event with an envelope, since the contract starts a new phase
choices.why: A start event creates an instance; this one already exists and is waiting in the middle.

choices.text: An end event with an envelope
choices.why: An end event consumes the token; the process continues after the contract arrives.

prompt: In Joana's first draft, the quality visit and the bank registration leave a parallel split and meet again at an exclusive gateway, followed by "approved?". What happens to an approved farm?
hint: Count the tokens that reach the second diamond.

choices.text: It is asked twice and sent two contracts
choices.why: Right: the exclusive join lets each of the two tokens through, so everything after it runs once per token.

choices.text: The engine refuses to deploy the model
choices.why: The pairing is legal BPMN; nothing stops it being deployed, which is why it is dangerous.

choices.text: Only the first branch to finish counts, so the bank account is lost
choices.why: An exclusive join does not discard the later token; it passes it through as well.

choices.text: It waits at the join for ever
choices.why: Waiting for ever is what a parallel join does after an exclusive split; this is the opposite pairing.

prompt: A process splits at an exclusive gateway and joins the two paths with a parallel gateway. In production, what does the operations team see for an affected instance?
hint: The join counts two incoming flows; how many tokens were made?

choices.text: An exception raised at the join, with the instance marked as failed
choices.why: Nothing fails: the join is behaving as specified, waiting for a token that was never created.

choices.text: An instance still running, nothing in any task list, and no error anywhere
choices.why: Right: a deadlock looks exactly like a slow instance, which is why testing for errors misses it.

choices.text: The step after the join running twice
choices.why: That is the parallel split joined by an exclusive gateway, the opposite mistake.

choices.text: Both paths taken, because the parallel join forces a token down each
choices.why: A join acts on tokens that arrive; it cannot reach back and create one on the path not taken.

prompt: A parallel gateway splits the flow into four branches, and the four branches are joined by an exclusive gateway. How many times does the task after the join run in one instance?
hint: One token per branch, and the exclusive join lets each one through.

prompt: After the document check, a farm far from any truck route needs a route survey, and a farm with an uncalibrated tank needs a tank inspection. Joana proposes an exclusive gateway with a default flow for "no extra checks". What goes wrong?
hint: A farm can need one, both or neither.

choices.text: A farm that needs neither check has nowhere to go
choices.why: The default flow is exactly what catches that case.

choices.text: Both checks run for every farm, whether it needs them or not
choices.why: That is what a parallel split would do; an exclusive one picks a single path.

choices.text: A farm that needs both gets only one
choices.why: Right: an exclusive split takes the first true condition and stops, so this needs an inclusive split and join.

choices.text: The join after the checks waits for ever for the branch that was not taken
choices.why: An exclusive split followed by an exclusive merge does not wait; that deadlock needs a parallel join.

prompt: Joana's second draft gave the farm a lane of its own, with a user task "Sign contract". Why did it become a pool?
hint: Think about what an engine does with a task in a lane.

choices.text: A lane stands for a department, and the farm is not one of Serra Alta's departments
choices.why: Lanes are roles inside a process, not departments; the farm is a pool because it runs its own process.

choices.text: A sequence flow cannot pass from one lane into another
choices.why: It can, and does every time work changes hands; only a pool boundary stops sequence flow.

choices.text: Serra Alta does not give the farm work; it sends it a contract and waits
choices.why: Right: a lane task would sit in Serra Alta's task list, so the exchange is a message out and a message back.

choices.text: Signing is a manual task, and lanes hold only user tasks
choices.why: Any kind of task can sit in a lane; the problem is who controls the work.

prompt: Which of these connections does BPMN allow? Choose all that apply.
hint: Sequence flow is order inside one process; message flow is between participants.

choices.text: A sequence flow from a task in the quality lane to a task in the finance lane
choices.why: Allowed: lanes are not boundaries, and work crossing them is what they show.

choices.text: A message flow between two tasks in the field team's lane
choices.why: Not allowed: both ends are in the same pool, where parts of a process are joined by sequence flow.

choices.text: A message flow from Serra Alta's send task to the edge of the farm's black-box pool
choices.why: Allowed: a message crossing between participants, landing on the edge because the pool is a black box.

choices.text: A sequence flow from Serra Alta's registration task into the bank's pool
choices.why: Not allowed: sequence flow never crosses a pool boundary; the bank is reached by messages.

prompt: In an executable model, a user task is drawn in the quality lane but its candidate group is set to finance. What happens when an instance reaches it?
hint: Which of the two does the engine read?

choices.text: The quality team gets it, because the lane takes precedence over the property
choices.why: Lanes carry no execution semantics in the standard; the engine never reads them for assignment.

choices.text: The engine refuses to deploy the model
choices.why: Nothing checks a lane against an assignment, so nothing refuses it.

choices.text: It appears in both task lists, and whoever claims it first does it
choices.why: There is one assignment, and the lane is not a second one.

choices.text: It goes to finance, and nothing reports the contradiction
choices.why: Right: the engine reads the task's own assignment, so keeping lanes and assignments in step is a review item.

prompt: For the farms onboarded in 2025, the work itself came to about four working days, and the median was 31 days. Where did the rest go?
hint: Look at the arrows that cross lane lines and pool edges.

choices.text: Into the engine, which ran the two parallel branches one after the other
choices.why: The branches really were parallel; the lost time is not inside the engine.

choices.text: Into queues at handoffs between lanes and waits on the other pools
choices.why: Right: every arrow crossing a lane is a queue and every message flow a wait outside Serra Alta's control.

choices.text: Into the quality visit itself, which takes most of a month at each farm
choices.why: The visit is part of the four days of work; the wait before a technician is free is not.

choices.text: Into retries of the bank registration, whose service times out
choices.why: Retries take minutes, not weeks, and the lesson found the time between lanes and pools.

prompt: Why is the 10-day timer on the quality visit non-interrupting?
hint: What happens to the visit task in each case?

choices.text: Every timer on a user task is non-interrupting
choices.why: A user task can carry either kind; an interrupting one would suit a response that replaces the task.

choices.text: A booked visit would be lost, so it stays open while Cláudia steps in
choices.why: Right: a dashed border starts a second path and leaves the activity running.

choices.text: An interrupting timer would end the whole onboarding instance
choices.why: It would cancel the activity it is attached to and follow its own path, not end the instance.

choices.text: A non-interrupting timer fires once, so the manager is not sent repeated tasks
choices.why: Firing once or repeatedly is the timer definition, a duration or a cycle, not the border.

prompt: A visit task carries a non-interrupting timer with the cycle R/P5D. The visit report arrives on day 17. How many reminders fired?
hint: List the days a five-day cycle fires on, up to the report.

prompt: In a timer definition, ten days written as an ISO 8601 duration is ___.
hint: P for period, then the number, then the unit.

prompt: A farm refuses the contract three weeks after its bank account was registered. Why does the model undo the registration with compensation rather than a rollback?
hint: Where and when was the registration committed?

choices.text: A rollback would also undo the quality visit, which has to be kept
choices.why: There is no transaction spanning the visit and the registration for a rollback to undo.

choices.text: Compensation is quicker, because it runs alongside the end event
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; a rollback is simply not available.

choices.text: BPMN engines keep no data in a database
choices.why: Engines do store their state in databases; the issue is the bank's system, not the engine's.

choices.text: It committed weeks ago in the bank's system, so reversing it takes a new action
choices.why: Right: no transaction stays open for weeks across organisations, so the undo is a separate step.

prompt: The bank's registration service does not answer within its timeout. What should the onboarding model do about it?
hint: Is there anything to tell the farm?

choices.text: Nothing new in the diagram: the engine retries the call and then raises an incident
choices.why: Right: a timeout is a technical failure with no business response, so it belongs to the engine's retries.

choices.text: Catch it with the error boundary event and ask the farm for its details again
choices.why: That path is for the bank rejecting the account; the farm's details may be fine.

choices.text: Throw compensation, in case the registration was half done
choices.why: Compensation undoes completed activities; this one has not completed.

choices.text: Add a non-interrupting timer that escalates to the finance manager
choices.why: A manager cannot make the bank answer; trying again in a few minutes is the response.

prompt: Even when SOAP was everywhere, why did WS-BPEL suit Serra Alta's onboarding badly?
hint: What is most of onboarding made of?

choices.text: It could not run two activities in parallel
choices.why: It could: `<flow>` runs activities in parallel.

choices.text: It had no way to wait for a message in the middle of a process
choices.why: A later `<receive>` with correlation does exactly that.

choices.text: Most of it is people, and every BPEL activity is a service call
choices.why: Right: human tasks needed BPEL4People or a vendor extension, and lost portability.

choices.text: It could not undo a completed step when something failed later
choices.why: Compensation handlers in a `<scope>` do that.

prompt: In WS-BPEL, the activity that calls an operation on a partner's web service is `<___>`.
hint: Its counterpart, which waits for a call, is `<receive>`.

prompt: Suppose onboarding were rebuilt so the field team's app, the quality app and the finance service each react to the others' events, and nothing runs the whole sequence. What would Joana and Denise lose?
hint: Orchestration or choreography, and what does each give you?

choices.text: Running the visit and the bank registration at the same time
choices.why: Participants reacting to the same event can work in parallel with no conductor.

choices.text: One place that knows where farm 4471's application is
choices.why: Right: a choreography leaves no participant holding the whole state, which is the question they care most about.

choices.text: The messages to the farm and to the bank
choices.why: Those are exchanged either way; they cross the boundary to other participants in both designs.

choices.text: Any way of undoing the bank registration when a contract is refused
choices.why: A choreography can undo it too, with a participant reacting to the refusal; it is just harder to see.

prompt: Which of these does the executable model have to carry that the diagram does not show?
hint: What would the engine need to evaluate at the gateway?

choices.text: The order of the tasks
choices.why: Order is exactly what the sequence flows on the diagram show.

choices.text: Which kind of gateway joins the two branches
choices.why: The marker inside the diamond shows that on the diagram.

choices.text: The places where the process can end
choices.why: End events are drawn, one per outcome.

choices.text: The expression that decides each flow out of a gateway
choices.why: Right: the diagram shows "yes" and "no"; the file needs a condition the engine can evaluate.

prompt: Denise keeps editing the onboarding diagram in her own tool while engineers add the bindings in the executable file. What does the lesson predict?
hint: Two copies of one process, edited by two groups.

choices.text: The engine merges the two versions when the model is deployed
choices.why: No engine merges a drawing tool's file with its own; it runs the file it is given.

choices.text: They drift: bindings vanish or point at the old structure
choices.why: Right: this is the round trip, and the cure is one model with one owner or two models that admit they differ.

choices.text: Nothing, because BPMN keeps business and technical parts in separate files
choices.why: One file holds both; only the diagram layout sits in a separate section of it.

choices.text: Denise's version wins, because the model is now the specification
choices.why: Being the specification does not make a second, edited copy agree with what runs.

prompt: Which of these is the weakest candidate for a process engine?
hint: Long, waiting on people and outsiders, with deadlines: or not?

choices.text: Working out an order's discount line by line inside the portal
choices.why: Right: that is one system's internal logic, which belongs in code where a test can reach it.

choices.text: Approving a new customer's credit, with a manager's review and a five-day deadline
choices.why: People, a wait and a deadline: an engine earns its keep here.

choices.text: Registering a new supplier, which waits for documents the supplier sends
choices.why: Waiting on an outside party for days is what engines are for.

choices.text: Recalling a batch, with tasks for quality, logistics and customer service
choices.why: Several teams, handoffs and a need to see each recall's state: a strong candidate.

prompt: Put the happy path of farm onboarding in order.
hint: Documents first, contract near the end.
items: Quality visit and bank registration, in parallel
Send the contract and wait for the signature
Create the farm in Coleta and SAP
trap: The bank registration does not wait for the visit report; the two run between the same pair of parallel gateways.

prompt: A colleague's model of supplier registration has the four features below. Which are defects, by this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Check each one against tokens, boundaries and waiting points.

choices.text: A parallel split closed by a parallel join
choices.why: Not a defect: the join waits for both tokens and the step after it runs once.

choices.text: A user task "Approve supplier" with no timer on it
choices.why: A defect: nothing says what happens if nobody approves, so an instance can wait for ever.

choices.text: A message flow from a task in the purchasing lane to a task in the finance lane
choices.why: A defect: both lanes are in one pool, so the connection is a sequence flow.

choices.text: An exclusive gateway with a default flow
choices.why: Not a defect: the default is what keeps an instance with no true condition from getting stuck.

prompt: Customer credit approval creates a credit limit in SAP, then a manager has five days to sign it off; if nobody signs, the request is cancelled. How should the wait be modelled?
hint: Two things race, and the loser has to leave nothing behind.

choices.text: A parallel gateway that waits for both the signature and the five days
choices.why: A parallel join would wait for both, so even a signed request would sit until day five.

choices.text: An error boundary event on the SAP task that fires after five days
choices.why: An error event catches a failure of the task it sits on, and the SAP task finished days earlier.

choices.text: A five-day timer racing the signature, whose timeout path compensates the limit
choices.why: Right: the race is the event-based gateway, or a timer on the sign-off task, and the timeout must undo the limit already created.

choices.text: An exclusive gateway whose condition checks whether five days have passed
choices.why: A gateway evaluates once, when the token arrives; it does not wait for time to pass.
